articles.title: Creatine may help build muscle even without exercise, researchers find
articles.summary: Creatine helped middle-aged adults gain muscle and strength even without a structured workout program in a new 12-week study. When combined with exercise and a calorie-reduced diet, it produced even greater strength gains while helping participants add lean tissue and lose fat. Researchers say the results strengthen the case for creatine as a potentially useful tool for maintaining muscle with age.
articles.content:
Creatine is widely known for helping support muscle growth and athletic performance, but researchers are increasingly examining whether its benefits extend well beyond the gym. New findings from Texas A&M University suggest creatine may be particularly useful in middle age, when preserving muscle becomes increasingly important.

In a 12-week study published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, adults ages 45 to 65 who took creatine increased their lean tissue and strength even if they did not follow a structured exercise program. Participants who combined creatine with regular exercise experienced even larger improvements.

The results add to growing research exploring creatine as more than a supplement for athletes. Scientists are also studying whether it can help support muscle health and healthy aging.

The study was led by Dr. Richard Kreider, professor and director of the Exercise and Sport Nutrition Lab at Texas A&M. Kreider has studied creatine for more than three decades. Creatine occurs naturally in the body and helps restore cellular energy, and decades of research have examined its effects on exercise performance, muscle growth, and strength. Kreider's earlier work has also suggested that creatine may offer health benefits throughout life.

Creatine Benefits Without Structured Exercise

The new study involved 64 healthy adults who completed the full 12-week intervention. Participants decided whether to join a structured exercise and diet-induced weight-loss program or remain in a non-exercise group. Within those groups, they were randomly assigned to consume either 10 grams of creatine monohydrate or a placebo each day.

Among participants who did not join the exercise program, those taking creatine gained roughly 2.4 pounds of lean tissue over the 12 weeks. They also increased their leg press and bench press strength.

Participants in the exercise program performed both resistance and aerobic training three times per week. Those who added creatine experienced greater gains in leg press strength, bench press strength, and time to exhaustion.

Creatine did not appear to improve aerobic capacity beyond the benefits of exercise alone. That result fits with previous evidence showing that creatine primarily supports muscular strength and power rather than aerobic fitness.

Building Muscle While Losing Fat

Researchers also examined another important issue: how to reduce body fat without losing muscle in the process.

Participants in the exercise group followed a diet that created a modest calorie deficit. After 12 weeks, those who took creatine had added nearly three pounds of lean tissue while also losing fat mass. By comparison, participants following the same exercise and diet program while taking a placebo showed little change in lean tissue.

The creatine group also experienced a larger decrease in body fat percentage. According to the researchers, this is the first study to show that adding creatine to an exercise and diet-induced weight-loss program can reduce body fat percentage more than exercise and diet alone.

Creatine and Healthy Aging

The findings add to decades of research investigating creatine for purposes beyond athletic performance.

Kreider has previously emphasized creatine's importance throughout the lifespan, including its potential value for older adults facing age-related declines in muscle mass and cognitive function.

The body makes creatine naturally, and it is also found in foods including meat and fish. However, Kreider says many people do not consume enough through food alone. Reaching a daily intake of 10 grams from diet alone would require eating roughly five to 10 pounds of meat or fish each day, he notes, making supplements a more practical and less costly option.

Creatine is also among the most heavily studied sports and nutritional supplements. In a 2025 analysis, Kreider and his colleagues reviewed 685 clinical trials and found no significant difference in reported side-effect rates between people taking creatine and those receiving a placebo.

The study was funded by the WoodNext Foundation through the Texas A&M Foundation.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a well-documented scientific study showing that creatine supplementation can help middle-aged adults build muscle and strength even without exercise, and enhances benefits when combined with exercise and diet. This has broad significance for healthy aging, muscle preservation, and fat loss, with potential to improve quality of life for a large population. The study is detailed and focused on a single important health topic with clear real-world impact.

articles.title: The ‘missed disease’ that affects 190 million: endometriosis drug shows early promise
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 01 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03042-xModified medication targets the cells implicated in the condition’s tell-tale lesions.
articles.content:
Endometriosis, a condition in which uterine cells form lesions outside of the uterus, has been termed the ‘missed disease’ owing to its unknown cause, delays in diagnosis and disparities in treatment.Credit: Zephyr/Science Photo Library

A new treatment for endometriosis — a painful, chronic condition that around 190 million people live with — might be on the horizon.

The disease is caused by cells of the inner lining of the uterus growing in parts of the body where they don’t belong. The resulting lesions are typically treated with surgery, hormone therapy or a combination of the two. These options come with various complications, however, and are often ineffective in the long term.

Could endometriosis be caused by bacteria? Study offers fresh clues

Now researchers have tweaked niclosamide, a drug used to treat parasitic infections such as tapeworms, to target cells implicated in the disease, and tested it in mice. The study is published in Advanced Healthcare Materials1.

If replicated in people, the results could provide a “breakthrough” in endometriosis treatment, says co-author Kanako Hayashi, a reproductive biologist at Washington State University in Pullman.

The study is a “beautiful first step” towards non-surgical, non-hormone-based therapies, says Elise Courtois, a molecular biologist at the Jackson Laboratory in Farmington, Connecticut.

When treatment misses the mark

Endometriosis can affect all those born with a uterus, and is most commonly diagnosed in girls and women between puberty and menopause.

People with the condition often experience severe abdominal and pelvic pain, that typically worsens during menstruation, as well as problems with fertility. The condition is underdiagnosed and undertreated, in part because it can be definitively diagnosed only with surgery to identify lesions outside the uterus. Other factors include the normalization of menstrual pain and the historical gender gap in health care.

Current treatments are far from adequate. Nearly half of people who undergo surgery to remove lesions — the gold-standard treatment — experience recurrence within five years. And hormone therapies are disruptive; they often prevent pregnancy, and side effects are wide-ranging and include depression, hot flushes and osteoporosis.

So researchers are looking for alternatives. In 2016, Hayashi worked on a study which found that niclosamide’s anti-inflammatory effects helped to attenuate the growth of endometrial tissue that had been implanted into mice2.

But there was a problem. Niclosamide isn’t well-absorbed in the body because of its low solubility in water. This means people must take high doses for it to work, and this often causes nausea, appetite loss and stomach cramps. In fact, the US Food and Drug Administration has approved niclosamide for use for only seven days at a time. That isn’t practical for treating a chronic condition.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a promising new drug treatment for endometriosis, a chronic condition affecting around 190 million people worldwide. The treatment targets the disease mechanism in a novel way, potentially offering a non-surgical, non-hormonal alternative that could significantly improve quality of life and treatment outcomes for a large and underserved patient population. The study has clear real-world impact, broad significance, and sufficient detail about the breakthrough.

articles.title: Is exposomics the key to making personalized medicine a reality?
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02958-8Scientists say tailored disease treatments require a comprehensive assessment of a person’s lifelong environmental exposures.
articles.content:
Researcher Ana Maretti Garcia collects transcriptomics data from clusters of cells exposed to ‘forever chemicals’.Credit: Gus Ruelas/USC

The year is 2050. During routine medical visits, patients provide blood and urine samples, their postal code and a description of their lifestyle and habits. The samples are analysed to detect nutrients and pharmaceuticals that the person has consumed, the bacterial and viral infections they have had and any chemicals they have encountered. Their location reveals key details about air pollution, noise and chemical exposure. By combining this information with the individual’s genome details, clinicians will be able to swiftly tally unique disease risks — as well as the actions or treatments that can best slow, or even quell, disease progression.

That’s the future that exposome researchers are working to create.

The exposome is the sum of environmental exposures and lifestyle factors that, in concert with genetics, shape the risk of a person developing many common conditions, including cancer, heart failure, diabetes and dementia. The term was coined in 2005 by Christopher Wild, a now-retired cancer epidemiologist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer in Lyon, France. He described a “desperate need to develop methods with the same precision for an individual’s environmental exposure as we have for the individual’s genome”1.

Nature Spotlight: Precision medicine

Environmental exposures are responsible for between 70% and 90% of the risk of developing chronic disease2. “Genetics load the gun, but the environment pulls the trigger,” said Francis Collins, former director of the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) in Bethesda, Maryland. Exposures can turn certain genes on or off, and these epigenetic changes can result in disease. For example, tobacco smoke can silence tumour-suppressor genes, increasing the risk of cancer.

Each individual’s exposure and genetic profile shapes their unique disease risks, and researchers say it is time to fill in the missing details. “If one does not address lifestyle factors, diet, medications, environmental exposures and other factors, care is not personalized,” says Gary Miller, director of the Center for Innovative Exposomics at Columbia University in New York City.

Exposomics research, however, is no small task. Any rigorous endeavour must offer a comprehensive assessment of as many non-genetic disease factors as possible. And understanding these will require researchers to collect and collate data from various sources, including biobanks and long-term cohort studies; surveys of diet, medications and physical activity; and environmental data sets such as geospatial models of air pollution.

Some exposures can be measured using biomarkers including sugars, proteins or chemical-breakdown products in the blood or urine that link biological changes to environmental triggers. “The signatures of past exposures stay in the body,” says Miller. Persistent organic pollutants, for example, leave a signature in fatty compounds called lipids in the blood. Smoking adds chemical tags, or epigenetic markers, to DNA, and these persist even if someone has not smoked for 30 years.

Advances in high-throughput mass spectrometry — a technique that allows scientists to analyse a large number of samples — have made it easier than ever to track proteins and metabolites in blood samples. This can be used alongside transcriptomics data, which shed light on the active genes in cells, to tease out and validate biochemical markers of disease from the cocktail of exposures.

Personalized CRISPR therapies could soon reach thousands — here’s how

Exposomics has its sceptics and misconceptions. Some critics suggest, for example, that it is simply a new term for an old discipline, environmental epidemiology (a field often focused on the impacts of individual exposures). Others say it is impossible to measure the totality of human exposures. Regardless, enthusiasm for exposomics has surged over the past decade. Searching the PubMed literature database for ‘exposome’ reveals that at least 830 papers have already been published this year, up from 261 in the whole of 2020.

Scientists are coordinating efforts to develop much-needed standards and protocols, and to create the capacity to continuously monitor dynamic exposures. Kyle Walsh, director of the US National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences in Research Triangle Park, North Carolina, says that there is growing enthusiasm at the NIH to fund a multi-year, multimillion-dollar Human Exposome Project, a comprehensive molecular-level assessment of the full suite of exposures to identify the most important drivers of disease.

If exposomics succeeds, it promises to usher in a new era of precision medicine — and precision prevention.

A quantified world

In March, Chirag Patel, an exposomics researcher at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts, and his colleagues published one of the largest studies yet to match exposures with disease risks3. The team compared 619 markers of exposure, ranging from blood mercury content to vitamin B12 levels, with 305 measurable characteristics, including lung function and blood sugar level, using data from ten cohorts of the 55-year-old US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Taken individually, environmental exposures accounted for less than 1% of the variation in disease outcomes, but that increased to an average of 3.5% when the researchers combined the effects of 20 exposures. It might not seem like a huge difference, but this figure rivals the predictive power of genetic variants that influence disease — and affirms the need to study real-life exposures to improve disease management, says Patel.

For example, 43% of participants’ triglyceride levels, a predictor of cardiovascular disease, were explained by a unique combination of 20 exposures — including trans fats and polychlorinated biphenyls. Advanced cellular ageing — structural or molecular damage to cells — was most strongly associated with smoking, minimal physical activity and exposure to heavy metals.

Patel says the next step is to find ways to narrow down which exposures are meaningful — the ones that perturb a biological pathway. If the link between environmental exposures and changes to biological pathways can be found at a population level, those results could be used to predict outcomes at an individual level, he says. A population study linking a cell mutation to an air pollutant could be used to identify people at risk of lung cancer, for example.

Personalized gene editing helped one baby: can it be rolled out widely?

This is where biobanked samples and cohort studies can prove pivotal. Walsh suggests that the All of Us programme, an NIH initiative to collect health data from more than one million US volunteers to accelerate precision medicine, is an obvious starting point for a Human Exposome Project. All of Us has so far enrolled 883,000 participants, making it the world’s largest integrated genomic and electronic health record database. It houses more than 600,000 physical measurements and 747,000 responses to surveys about social circumstances, behaviour and environment.

The fundamental challenge is to connect all the dots to understand how that information translates into an individual’s disease risk. “It’s a data-analysis problem,” says Walsh. But he says it will become much more tractable courtesy of artificial-intelligence tools.

High-resolution mass spectrometry on blood or urine samples typically returns a spectrum with 10,000 to 100,000 distinct peaks. Identifying — and quantifying — which chemical compounds correspond to the peaks is one of the biggest bottlenecks in exposomics. However, machine-learning models can sift through the data to decode them with ease. Furthermore, they can predict adverse biological effects from a chemical’s structure, which will allow researchers to include as-yet-unknown chemicals in disease-risk assessments.

As AI tools are adopted, researchers are eager to increase the scale and scope of projects. Miller predicts that in the next three years, scientists will conduct a state-of-the-art exposomics study using data from around 100,000 people. “If we did that across ten major human diseases, we would see which exposome profiles are related to different outcomes in different diseases.” And that could help clinicians to determine whose disease will progress fastest, or who will see the most improvement from taking one drug or another.

Towards prevention

The clinical potential of exposomics is starting to come into focus. The Exposome-Scan facility in Leiden, the Netherlands, launched in 2024 to create exposome profiles for researchers and clinicians. At the moment, it can identify roughly 700 chemicals in exposome scans — including pesticides and flame retardants, says Roel Vermeulen, an exposome researcher at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, who co-leads the facility. He estimates that this is roughly 10–20% of the few thousand chemicals that lead to significant exposures in people globally. “I strongly believe that we should not wait until we can measure everything,” he says.

This research has broad implications for improving disease prevention and treatment for many common chronic diseases, representing a meaningful advancement in health science with potential large-scale benefits. The article provides detailed context about the challenges, methodologies, and future prospects, demonstrating substantive progress toward a transformative healthcare approach.
articles.personality_title: New science tracks lifelong exposures to personalize medicine by 2050
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists are working to understand how a person’s environment and lifestyle, combined with their genes, affect their chances of getting diseases like cancer, diabetes, and heart problems. This field of study is called exposomics, which looks at all the things people are exposed to during their lives, such as pollution, chemicals, infections, and diet.

**What happened** – Researchers have made progress in measuring many environmental exposures using blood and urine tests, advanced lab tools, and data from large health studies. They can now detect chemicals and biological markers that show how these exposures change the body. Studies have linked groups of exposures with disease risks, showing they can be as important as genes. Scientists plan big projects like the Human Exposome Project to collect even more detailed data from hundreds of thousands of people.

**Impact** – This work is important because it moves medicine beyond just looking at genes to also consider the environment around each person. By understanding all the exposures that influence health, doctors could predict who is likely to develop certain diseases and choose treatments that work best for each individual. This could help slow down or even prevent diseases by targeting the right causes.

**What's next step** – Researchers aim to use artificial intelligence to analyze vast amounts of exposure data and identify the most important factors affecting health. Large studies with tens of thousands of participants are planned to connect specific exposure patterns to different diseases. This will help doctors tailor treatments and prevention strategies more precisely.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists are building tools to measure lifelong environmental exposures alongside genes, paving the way for truly personalized medicine by 2050.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle science suit les expositions tout au long de la vie pour personnaliser la médecine d'ici 2050
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques cherchent à comprendre comment l’environnement et le mode de vie d’une personne, combinés à ses gènes, influencent ses risques de développer des maladies comme le cancer, le diabète ou les problèmes cardiaques. Ce domaine d’étude s’appelle l’exposomique, qui analyse toutes les expositions vécues au cours de la vie, comme la pollution, les produits chimiques, les infections et l’alimentation.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Les chercheurs ont progressé dans la mesure de nombreuses expositions environnementales grâce à des analyses de sang et d’urine, des outils de laboratoire avancés et des données issues de grandes études de santé. Ils peuvent désormais détecter des produits chimiques et des marqueurs biologiques montrant comment ces expositions modifient le corps. Des études ont relié des groupes d’expositions aux risques de maladie, montrant qu’elles peuvent être aussi importantes que les gènes. De grands projets comme le Human Exposome Project sont prévus pour collecter des données encore plus détaillées auprès de centaines de milliers de personnes.

**Impact** – Ce travail est important car il va au-delà de l’étude des seuls gènes pour prendre en compte l’environnement de chaque personne. En comprenant toutes les expositions qui influencent la santé, les médecins pourraient mieux prédire qui risque de développer certaines maladies et choisir les traitements les plus adaptés. Cela pourrait aider à ralentir ou même prévenir les maladies en ciblant les bonnes causes.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent utiliser l’intelligence artificielle pour analyser d’énormes quantités de données sur les expositions et identifier les facteurs les plus importants pour la santé. De grandes études impliquant des dizaines de milliers de participants sont prévues pour relier des profils d’exposition spécifiques à différentes maladies. Cela aidera les médecins à adapter les traitements et les stratégies de prévention.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les scientifiques développent des outils pour mesurer les expositions environnementales tout au long de la vie avec les gènes, ouvrant la voie à une médecine vraiment personnalisée d’ici 2050.
articles.personality_title_es: Nueva ciencia rastrea exposiciones de por vida para personalizar la medicina para 2050
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos están trabajando para entender cómo el ambiente y el estilo de vida de una persona, junto con sus genes, afectan sus probabilidades de desarrollar enfermedades como cáncer, diabetes y problemas cardíacos. Este campo de estudio se llama exposómica, que analiza todas las exposiciones que una persona tiene durante su vida, como la contaminación, productos químicos, infecciones y dieta.

**Qué pasó** – Los investigadores han avanzado en medir muchas exposiciones ambientales usando análisis de sangre y orina, herramientas de laboratorio avanzadas y datos de grandes estudios de salud. Ahora pueden detectar químicos y marcadores biológicos que muestran cómo estas exposiciones cambian el cuerpo. Estudios han relacionado grupos de exposiciones con riesgos de enfermedad, mostrando que pueden ser tan importantes como los genes. Se planean grandes proyectos como el Human Exposome Project para recopilar datos aún más detallados de cientos de miles de personas.

**Impacto** – Este trabajo es importante porque lleva la medicina más allá del estudio solo de genes para incluir el ambiente de cada persona. Al comprender todas las exposiciones que influyen en la salud, los médicos podrían predecir quién es más propenso a ciertas enfermedades y elegir los tratamientos que mejor funcionen para cada individuo. Esto podría ayudar a ralentizar o incluso prevenir enfermedades al atacar las causas correctas.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores planean usar inteligencia artificial para analizar grandes cantidades de datos de exposiciones e identificar los factores más importantes para la salud. Se planean estudios grandes con decenas de miles de participantes para conectar patrones específicos de exposición con diferentes enfermedades. Esto ayudará a los médicos a personalizar tratamientos y estrategias de prevención.

**Frase resumen** – Los científicos están creando herramientas para medir las exposiciones ambientales de por vida junto con los genes, preparando el camino para una medicina verdaderamente personalizada para 2050.

articles.title: AI ‘speech clock’ assesses how fast you’re ageing from your voice
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03106-yThe pitch and emotional content of your speech are important predictors of accelerated ageing, researchers find.
articles.content:
A new ‘speech clock’ analyses characteristics of a person’s voice, including pitch, to assess how quickly they are ageing.Credit: Cheschhh/Getty

A ‘speech clock’ developed by scientists can predict how well a person is ageing based on characteristics of their voice and how they talk. The clock draws on hundreds of vocal features, including pitch and talking speed, to estimate a person’s age.

‘Inflammation clock’ can reveal body’s biological age

Using the clock, the scientists calculated a ‘speech age gap’ for individuals: the difference between a person’s age as predicted by the speech clock and their chronological age. Large speech age gaps were strongly associated with cognitive issues in people, such as those that arise in dementia, suggesting that the new clock could be a useful tool for determining whether a person is growing older faster than expected.

The findings were published today in the journal Science Advances1.

“We can see a huge predictive value, just with a very simple four minutes of speech recordings,” says neuroscientist Agustín Ibáñez at Adolfo Ibáñez University in Santiago, who is a co-author of the study.

The speech clock could be a boon for tracking the ageing of people in low-resource regions, because it doesn’t rely on expensive or invasive technologies, such as brain scans and blood tests, says Jed Meltzer, a cognitive neuroscientist who specializes in language at the University of Toronto in Canada and was not involved in the study. “It is a very impressive piece of work.”

Predicting age with speech

Ageing clocks often use biological markers to assess how rapidly a person’s body is declining. For instance, ‘brain clocks’ use signatures from neuroimaging to determine whether an individual’s brain is ageing faster than their chronological age suggests. And ‘epigenetic clocks’ look at the patterns of methyl tags on a person’s DNA to estimate their biological age. But so far, researchers hadn’t developed a clock based on speech. Such a tool could offer a useful window into the ageing process because speaking involves a “huge amount of brain work”, Ibáñez says.

How quickly are you ageing? What molecular ‘clocks’ can tell you about your health

To create their clock, Ibáñez and his colleagues recorded 2,928 Spanish speakers from Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru while they completed various speech tasks. The group was a mixture of healthy individuals and people with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer’s disease or other forms of dementia. The researchers used machine-learning algorithms to extract more than 700 speech characteristics that can change with ageing and dementia, such as pitch and vocabulary range, from the audio recordings. They then used these data to train their speech-clock model to predict each study participant’s age.

Overall, the speech clock could distinguish between healthy individuals and those with some form of cognitive impairment. The clock, for instance, categorized the speech of people with cognitive issues as being older than would be expected for their chronological age. Healthy people were generally assessed as having speech that matched their chronological age.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a novel scientific breakthrough—a speech-based ageing clock that can non-invasively and affordably assess biological ageing and cognitive decline. This has broad potential health benefits, especially for early detection of dementia and ageing-related conditions, and is significant for populations with limited access to expensive medical tests. The study is detailed and focused on a single impactful innovation.
articles.personality_title: New ‘speech clock’ uses your voice to measure how fast you’re ageing
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have been working on ways to measure how fast a person is ageing using biological signs. These methods often require expensive tests or scans. Now, researchers have developed a new tool that uses just a person’s voice to estimate their biological age.

**What happened** – A team of scientists recorded the voices of nearly 3,000 Spanish-speaking people from several countries. They used computers to analyze hundreds of features in the recordings, like pitch and speaking speed, to create a ‘speech clock’. This clock compares the predicted age from the voice to the person’s real age. They found that people with faster ageing or cognitive problems, such as dementia, tend to have a bigger difference between these ages.

**Impact** – This voice-based ageing test is important because it is simple, non-invasive, and affordable. It can help detect early signs of ageing and brain problems without needing costly medical equipment. This makes it especially useful in places where access to health care is limited. It also shows that changes in speech can give clues about brain health.

**What's next step** – Researchers hope to test this speech clock in more languages and different groups of people. They also want to see if it can help doctors track ageing and cognitive health over time. The tool may be used in the future to spot early signs of conditions like Alzheimer’s disease.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists created a new tool that listens to your voice to tell how fast you are ageing and if your brain health might be at risk.
articles.personality_title_fr: Nouvelle « horloge vocale » mesure la vitesse de votre vieillissement grâce à votre voix
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques cherchent des moyens de mesurer la vitesse à laquelle une personne vieillit en utilisant des signes biologiques. Ces méthodes demandent souvent des tests ou des scanners coûteux. Aujourd’hui, des chercheurs ont développé un nouvel outil qui utilise uniquement la voix pour estimer l’âge biologique.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe a enregistré la voix de près de 3 000 personnes hispanophones de plusieurs pays. Ils ont utilisé des ordinateurs pour analyser des centaines de caractéristiques dans les enregistrements, comme la hauteur et la vitesse de parole, pour créer une « horloge vocale ». Cette horloge compare l’âge prédit par la voix à l’âge réel de la personne. Ils ont constaté que ceux qui vieillissent plus vite ou ont des problèmes cognitifs, comme la démence, ont une plus grande différence entre ces âges.

**Impact** – Ce test basé sur la voix est important car il est simple, non invasif et peu coûteux. Il peut aider à détecter tôt le vieillissement et les problèmes cérébraux sans matériel médical cher. Cela est particulièrement utile dans les régions où l’accès aux soins est limité. Cela montre aussi que la parole peut donner des indices sur la santé du cerveau.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent tester cette horloge vocale dans d’autres langues et groupes de personnes. Ils souhaitent aussi voir si elle peut aider les médecins à suivre le vieillissement et la santé cognitive au fil du temps. Cet outil pourrait servir à détecter tôt des maladies comme Alzheimer.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des scientifiques ont créé un outil qui écoute votre voix pour mesurer la vitesse de votre vieillissement et détecter des risques pour votre cerveau.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo ‘reloj de voz’ mide qué tan rápido envejeces solo escuchando tu voz
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han buscado formas de medir qué tan rápido envejece una persona usando señales biológicas. Estos métodos suelen requerir pruebas o escáneres costosos. Ahora, investigadores desarrollaron una herramienta que usa solo la voz para estimar la edad biológica.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo grabó las voces de casi 3,000 personas hispanohablantes de varios países. Usaron computadoras para analizar cientos de características en las grabaciones, como el tono y la velocidad al hablar, para crear un ‘reloj de voz’. Este reloj compara la edad que predice la voz con la edad real del individuo. Encontraron que quienes envejecen más rápido o tienen problemas cognitivos, como demencia, muestran una mayor diferencia entre estas edades.

**Impacto** – Esta prueba basada en la voz es importante porque es simple, no invasiva y económica. Puede ayudar a detectar señales tempranas de envejecimiento y problemas cerebrales sin necesidad de equipos médicos caros. Esto es especialmente útil en lugares con poco acceso a atención médica. También demuestra que el habla puede dar pistas sobre la salud del cerebro.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores esperan probar este reloj de voz en más idiomas y diferentes grupos de personas. También quieren ver si puede ayudar a los médicos a seguir el envejecimiento y la salud cognitiva con el tiempo. La herramienta podría usarse para detectar temprano enfermedades como el Alzheimer.

**Resumen en una frase** – Científicos crearon una herramienta que escucha tu voz para medir qué tan rápido envejeces y si tu salud cerebral está en riesgo.
